title: Data in a table
summary: Data analysis starts with a table. A CSV file is a table saved as plain text, one row per line and commas between the values. pandas reads it in one line with pd.read_csv() into a DataFrame: named columns, numbered rows.
objectives: Say what a CSV file is and how it maps to a table.
Read a CSV file into a DataFrame with pd.read_csv().
Show the first and last rows with head() and tail().
Show just a few columns of the table.

lecture.title: A table in a text file

slides.h: By the end: a whole season in one variable
slides.say: Every row of players.csv is one player of a T20 league season: team, role, matches, runs, balls faced, fours, sixes and wickets. The league is made up, so every number is practice data. By the end of this lesson you’ll have all of it in one variable.
points: A **CSV** (comma-separated values) file is plain text: the first line holds the column names, each other line is one row.
`import pandas as pd` loads pandas, the library everyone uses for tables.
p: Every row of players.csv is one player of a T20 league season: team, role, matches, runs, balls faced, fours, sixes and wickets. The league is made up, so every number is practice data. By the end of this lesson you’ll have all of it in one variable.

terms: a table saved as text, values separated by commas
the Python library for tables of data
a table in pandas: named columns, numbered rows

slides.say: The first line became the column names. Every other line became a row, numbered from **0** down the left: that number is the **index**. Numbers came in as numbers, so you can add them up straight away.
points: The index isn’t one of your columns; pandas adds it.
Row 0 is the first player, not the header.
Text with a comma inside is put in quotes in the file, so it stays one value.

slides.say: A real file can have a million rows, so you rarely print all of it. `head()` shows the first 5 rows, `tail()` the last 5; put a number in the brackets for more or fewer.
points: A wide table is cut with `...` in the middle; pick the columns you want to see.

slides.say: One column name in square brackets gives that column. A **list** of names, so two pairs of brackets, gives a smaller table with just those columns, in the order you list them.
points: Names must match exactly, capitals included: "runs" isn’t "Runs".

options: pandas is used as pd from now on

points: A CSV file is a table as text: a header line, then one line per row.
`df = pd.read_csv("file.csv")` gives a DataFrame; the index numbers rows from 0.
`df.head(n)` and `df.tail(n)` show the first and last rows.
`df["Col"]` is one column; `df[["A", "B"]]` is a table of those columns. Names are exact.

cards.front: What is the index of the first row?
cards.back: 0: pandas numbers rows from 0; the header gives the column names.
Column names are exact, capitals included: "Runs".
